scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

This isn’t just about "knowing"—it’s about **how you went about it**. --- ### **2. Was Your Approach Justified?** - **Pros of Your Stance:** - You were acting from **love and concern** for your son’s well-being. Pushing for disclosure can feel like **parental overreach**, especially if he’s otherwise healthy and active. - **The "why" isn’t always the point**: Therapy often explores **processes** (e.g., coping skills, emotional regulation) rather than a single "reason." The goal is his well-being, not control. --- ### **3. This isn’t about "being right"—it’s about **how you treated him**. --- ### **4. What Should You Do Now?** - **Repair the relationship**: - Apologize to your son for **overstepping** and **not trusting him**. I realize I pushed too hard about therapy, and I’m sorry I made you feel like I didn’t trust you. I’m here to listen if you ever want to talk."* - Give him space to respond—don’t force conversation. - **Work with the therapist collaboratively**: - Ask the therapist for **general progress updates** (e.g., "Is he showing improvement in [specific area]?"). Frame it as **supporting your son’s process**, not as an interrogation. - If possible, **attend a session together** (with your son’s consent) to build trust. Many therapists welcome this if the teen agrees. - **Re-evaluate your assumptions**: - Your son is 17—he may be dealing with **identity, pressure, or social challenges** that don’t fit your preconceived notions (e.g., anxiety, LGBTQ+ struggles, academic stress). Don’t dismiss his reasons just because they don’t match your initial guesses. - **Men’s mental health** is often stigmatized, and he might be hesitant to open up about emotions. Therapy could be helping him navigate that. - **Focus on the bigger picture**: - The goal isn’t to "win" the argument or "get answers"—it’s to **support your son’s well-being**. If he’s attending therapy and seems to benefit, that’s a success, even if you don’t understand the "why" yet. --- ### **5. Ethical Scorecard (0–1 Scale)** If we assign a **0 (wrong) to 1 (right)** scale based on **intent, impact, and ethical alignment**, your actions would likely fall in the **0.3–0.5 range**—**not wrong, but flawed**. - **Intent (0.8/1)**: You were acting from care, not malice. - **Ethical Alignment (0.2/1)**: Violated therapist-client confidentiality and autonomy. - **Impact (0.4/1)**: Damaged trust with your son, which could harm his therapy. - **Alternative Approach (0.6/1)**: There were better ways to get information without violating boundaries. **Final Verdict**: You weren’t "assholes" in the malicious sense, but your approach **crossed ethical lines** and had **negative consequences**. The key takeaway is that **parental concern must be balanced with respect for your child’s autonomy and the therapeutic process**. --- ### **Key Takeaway for Parents** When your child seeks help (especially in therapy), **trust the process** more than your need for control. Therapy works best when the client feels **safe and respected**. Your role as a parent is to **support**, not interrogate.
